dx: Mumps parotitis in an unvaccinated college student
case: A 19-year-old man comes to the student health clinic because of a 2-day history of painful swelling at both angles of the jaw and pain with chewing. Fever, malaise, and headache began 3 days earlier. He did not receive childhood vaccinations, and several students in his residence hall have had a similar illness. Temperature is 38.4 °C (101.1 °F), pulse is 92/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg. Physical examination shows tender, bilateral parotid swelling that obscures the angles of the mandible. The parotid duct openings are erythematous, and no pus is expressed with gland massage. The testes are normal. Serum amylase concentration is 310 U/L (normal 25 to 125), and serum lipase concentration is 48 U/L (normal 10 to 140). RT-PCR of a buccal swab detects mumps virus. Diagnosis: mumps parotitis.

questions.stem: During the same week, a 76-year-old man who is dehydrated 4 days after a colectomy develops painful swelling of the right parotid gland and a temperature of 38.6 °C (101.5 °F). Which of the following findings would best distinguish his condition from that of the college student?
options: Raised serum amylase with a normal lipase concentration
Pain in the gland that worsens with chewing
Pus expressed from the parotid duct opening
Swelling that obscures the angle of the mandible
approach: Recognize the older patient's setting: postoperative, dehydrated, one gland involved. This points to acute bacterial parotitis.
List what both conditions share: a swollen, tender parotid, pain with chewing, fever, and a raised salivary amylase.
Pick the finding seen only with bacterial infection: pus at the duct opening.
questions.why: Acute bacterial parotitis develops when salivary flow falls, as with dehydration after surgery, and bacteria ascend the parotid (Stensen) duct. Staphylococcus aureus is the usual cause. The gland fills with neutrophils, so massaging it pushes pus out of the duct opening. Mumps is a viral infection of the gland tissue, so the duct openings may be red, but no pus comes out.
whyNot: Any inflamed salivary gland leaks salivary-type amylase into the blood while lipase stays normal. This pattern points to the salivary glands but does not tell viral from bacterial disease.
Chewing stimulates salivary secretion and stretches the inflamed gland capsule, so it hurts in both mumps and bacterial parotitis.
Correct.
Marked swelling hides the angle of the mandible whenever the parotid enlarges, whatever the cause.

questions.stem: His roommate, a 22-year-old man, has recurrent painful swelling below the left side of the mandible that begins within minutes of eating and subsides over the next hour. Radiography shows a radiopaque calculus in the floor of the mouth. Which of the following features of the affected gland best explains why calculi form most often in this gland?
options: Thicker, mucin-rich saliva drained upward through a long duct
Mainly serous, amylase-rich saliva drained through a short duct
A duct that opens opposite the upper second molar tooth
Many small ducts that open along the sublingual fold
approach: Locate the swelling: below the mandible with a stone in the floor of the mouth means the submandibular gland and its duct.
Recall the two features that favor stone formation in this gland: viscous saliva and a long duct that runs upward against gravity.
Link slow flow of thick saliva to precipitation of calcium salts.
questions.why: About 80 to 90% of salivary stones form in the submandibular gland. Its saliva is a mixed serous and mucous secretion that is more viscous and more alkaline, with more calcium, than parotid saliva. Its duct (Wharton duct) is long and runs upward and forward to open beside the frenulum of the tongue, so saliva drains against gravity and stagnates. A stone blocks outflow, so the gland swells and hurts when eating stimulates secretion, and stagnant saliva can become infected (sialadenitis).
whyNot: Correct.
This describes the parotid gland. Thin serous saliva flows easily, which is one reason parotid stones are uncommon.
The parotid (Stensen) duct opens on the inner cheek opposite the upper second molar. A stone there would cause swelling in front of the ear.
The sublingual gland drains through many small ducts in the sublingual fold. Short ducts with little stasis make stones in this gland rare.

questions.stem: His raised serum amylase comes from the inflamed glands. Which of the following best describes the secretory units that make up nearly all of these glands?
options: Mucous acini that secrete a viscous, mucin-rich fluid
Mixed acini of mucous cells capped by serous demilunes
Exocrine acini with scattered islets of endocrine cells
Serous acini that secrete a watery, amylase-rich fluid
approach: Identify the glands involved: the parotid glands.
Recall that the parotid is an almost purely serous gland.
Connect serous cells to their product, salivary amylase, which explains the raised serum amylase.
questions.why: The parotid gland is made almost entirely of serous acini. Serous cells have basophilic cytoplasm, round central nuclei, and apical secretory granules, and they make a watery fluid rich in salivary amylase. When mumps virus inflames the parotid, this amylase leaks into the blood. The submandibular gland is mixed but mostly serous, and the sublingual gland is mostly mucous.
whyNot: Mucous acini, with pale, foamy cytoplasm and flattened basal nuclei, make up most of the sublingual gland and the minor salivary glands of the palate.
Mucous tubules capped by serous demilunes are typical of the submandibular and sublingual glands.
Acini mixed with islets of Langerhans describe the pancreas. Mumps can inflame the pancreas, but his normal lipase points away from it.
Correct.

questions.stem: Mumps virus first replicates in the upper respiratory mucosa. After recovery, his saliva contains the main antibody class that protects mucosal surfaces. Which of the following mediates the transport of this antibody into his saliva?
options: Neonatal Fc receptor carrying IgG across the epithelium
Polymeric Ig receptor on the basolateral epithelial surface
M cell transcytosis of antigen to underlying lymphoid follicles
Passive leakage of plasma IgM between epithelial cells
approach: Name the antibody in saliva and other mucosal secretions: secretory IgA.
Recall how it crosses the epithelium: plasma cells under the epithelium release dimeric IgA joined by a J chain, and epithelial cells carry it across.
Match this to the polymeric immunoglobulin receptor.
questions.why: Plasma cells in the gland stroma and mucosa secrete IgA as a dimer held together by a J chain. The polymeric immunoglobulin receptor on the basolateral surface of epithelial cells binds the dimer and carries it across the cell by transcytosis. At the apical surface the receptor is cleaved, and the piece that stays attached, called secretory component, protects IgA from digestion in the secretions. Secretory IgA blocks viruses and bacteria from attaching to mucosal cells.
whyNot: The neonatal Fc receptor carries IgG across the placenta and protects IgG from breakdown, which gives IgG its long half-life. It is not the route for antibody in saliva.
Correct.
M cells over Peyer patches carry antigen from the gut lumen to lymphoid tissue to start mucosal immune responses. They move antigen inward, not antibody outward.
IgM can also be carried by the polymeric Ig receptor, but it is a minor secretory antibody, and it moves by active transcytosis, not leakage.

dx: Pleomorphic adenoma of the parotid gland
case: A 46-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a painless lump in front of her right ear that has grown slowly over 3 years. She has no facial weakness, numbness, or pain. Temperature is 36.8 °C (98.2 °F), pulse is 72/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 124/78 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a 2.5-cm, firm, mobile, nontender mass in the superficial part of the right parotid gland. Facial nerve function is normal on both sides. There is no cervical lymphadenopathy. Fine-needle aspiration shows epithelial and myoepithelial cells in a myxoid and chondroid stroma. She undergoes superficial parotidectomy. Diagnosis: pleomorphic adenoma of the right parotid gland.

questions.stem: Her surgeon removes the tumor with a margin of normal gland tissue and avoids simple enucleation. Which of the following features of this tumor best explains this choice?
options: Cystic spaces lined by oncocytes over lymphoid stroma
Finger-like projections through an incomplete capsule
Perineural invasion along branches of the facial nerve
Infiltrating mixture of mucus-secreting and squamoid cells
approach: Recognize the most common salivary tumor: a slow-growing, mobile parotid mass with epithelial, myoepithelial, and chondromyxoid tissue.
Recall that this benign tumor is not fully encapsulated.
Connect the small extensions of tumor beyond the capsule to recurrence when the tumor is shelled out.
questions.why: Pleomorphic adenoma is the most common salivary gland tumor, and most arise in the parotid. It is benign and mixes epithelial and myoepithelial cells with myxoid, hyaline, or cartilage-like stroma. The capsule is incomplete, and small tongues of tumor push into the surrounding gland. Shelling out the main mass leaves these projections behind, so recurrence is common unless a rim of normal tissue is removed. Long-standing tumors carry a small risk of malignant change.
whyNot: Oncocytic cysts over dense lymphoid stroma describe Warthin tumor, the second most common benign parotid tumor, which is strongly linked to smoking. Its cytology differs from this aspirate.
Correct.
Perineural invasion is the hallmark of adenoid cystic carcinoma, a malignant tumor that often causes pain or facial weakness. Her nerve function is normal and the aspirate shows a benign mixed tumor.
Mucus-secreting, squamoid, and intermediate cells describe mucoepidermoid carcinoma, the most common malignant salivary tumor.

questions.stem: During the operation, the surgeon identifies and preserves a nerve that branches within the gland, between its superficial and deep parts. Injury to this nerve would most likely cause which of the following?
options: Numbness of the skin over the right angle of the mandible
Reduced secretion of saliva from the right parotid gland
Deviation of the jaw to the right on opening the mouth
Weak right eye closure and a drooping mouth corner
approach: Identify the nerve that divides into its branches inside the parotid gland: the facial nerve (CN VII).
Recall what the facial nerve does after it leaves the stylomastoid foramen: it supplies the muscles of facial expression.
Predict weakness of the orbicularis oculi and the muscles of the mouth on the same side.
questions.why: After leaving the stylomastoid foramen, the facial nerve enters the parotid gland and divides into its temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular, and cervical branches within it. The plane of the nerve separates the superficial part of the gland from the deep part. These branches carry only motor fibers to the muscles of facial expression, so injury weakens eye closure and lets the corner of the mouth droop on that side. This is why a parotid mass that causes facial weakness raises concern for a malignant tumor.
whyNot: Skin over the angle of the mandible is supplied by the great auricular nerve (C2 and C3), which can be cut during parotid surgery but runs on the surface of the gland, not through it.
Secretomotor fibers to the parotid come from CN IX through the otic ganglion and reach the gland with the auriculotemporal nerve. The facial nerve branches in the gland do not carry them.
The muscles of mastication, including the lateral pterygoid that opens the jaw, are supplied by CN V3. Weakness of one lateral pterygoid makes the jaw deviate toward the weak side.
Correct.

topics: Facial nerve in the parotid gland

questions.stem: Five years later, she receives radiation therapy for an unrelated oropharyngeal cancer, and both parotid glands are in the radiation field. Over the next year, her mouth stays dry, and she develops many new carious lesions along the gum line. Loss of which of the following salivary functions most directly explains the new dental caries?
options: Bicarbonate buffering of acid from plaque bacteria
Lingual lipase hydrolysis of dietary triglycerides
Amylase digestion of dietary starch into maltose
Haptocorrin binding of dietary vitamin B12
approach: Recognize that radiation has destroyed the serous acini, so salivary flow has fallen.
Recall how caries form: plaque bacteria ferment sugars to acid, which dissolves enamel.
Choose the salivary function that neutralizes this acid.
questions.why: Saliva protects the teeth in several ways. Its bicarbonate buffers the acid that plaque bacteria such as Streptococcus mutans make from dietary sugar, and its calcium and phosphate help remineralize enamel. It also contains IgA, lysozyme, and lactoferrin that limit bacterial growth, and its flow washes the teeth. When salivary flow falls, as after radiation or in Sjogren syndrome, acid stays on the enamel and caries develop quickly, often at the gum line.
whyNot: Correct.
Lingual lipase begins fat digestion, mainly in infants. It has no protective role for the teeth.
Salivary amylase starts starch digestion. Its loss would not promote caries, and breaking starch into sugars actually gives plaque bacteria more substrate.
Haptocorrin (R binder) protects vitamin B12 from stomach acid. It has no role in protecting enamel.

questions.stem: Before surgery, her swallowing is evaluated. When a swallowed bolus enters the pharynx, her lower esophageal sphincter relaxes before the peristaltic wave reaches it. Which of the following most directly mediates this relaxation?
options: Vagal excitatory neurons releasing acetylcholine
Sympathetic fibers releasing norepinephrine onto beta-2 receptors
Vagal inhibitory neurons releasing nitric oxide and VIP
Gastrin released from antral G cells after the meal
approach: Recall that the pharyngeal phase of swallowing is a reflex coordinated by the swallowing center in the medulla.
Recognize that the sphincter must open ahead of the bolus, which needs active inhibition of its tonic contraction.
Identify the inhibitory transmitters released by vagal pathways in the myenteric plexus: nitric oxide and VIP.
questions.why: Swallowing starts voluntarily in the mouth, and the pharyngeal and esophageal phases then run as a reflex organized in the medulla. Through the vagus nerve, the swallowing center activates inhibitory neurons in the myenteric plexus of the esophagus and stomach. These neurons release nitric oxide and vasoactive intestinal peptide, which relax the smooth muscle of the lower esophageal sphincter and the proximal stomach (receptive relaxation). Loss of these inhibitory neurons causes achalasia.
whyNot: Acetylcholine from vagal excitatory neurons contracts esophageal smooth muscle and drives peristalsis. It does not relax the sphincter.
Sympathetic input has little role in swallowing and does not produce the rapid relaxation that precedes the bolus.
Correct.
Gastrin increases lower esophageal sphincter tone, and it is released only after food reaches the stomach.

dx: Acute alcohol-related pancreatitis complicated by a pseudocyst
case: A 42-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of a 1-day history of severe epigastric pain that radiates to the back, with nausea and vomiting. He has drunk about 10 beers daily for 15 years and drank heavily for 2 days before the pain began. Temperature is 38.1 °C (100.6 °F), pulse is 112/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 104/66 mm Hg. Physical examination shows epigastric tenderness with guarding and decreased bowel sounds. Serum lipase concentration is 1850 U/L (normal 10 to 140), and serum calcium concentration is 8.6 mg/dL (normal 8.5 to 10.5). Ultrasonography shows no gallstones. CT shows an edematous pancreas with peripancreatic fluid. Diagnosis: acute alcohol-related pancreatitis. Five weeks later, he has early satiety and epigastric fullness, and CT shows a 7-cm, well-defined fluid collection in the lesser sac behind the stomach.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the key initiating event in the pathogenesis of his pancreatic injury?
options: Activation of trypsinogen to trypsin within acinar cells
Release of insulin and glucagon from destroyed islet cells
Reflux of bile into the pancreatic duct through a common channel
IgG4-positive plasma cells infiltrating and destroying acini
approach: Recall that pancreatic enzymes are normally made as inactive zymogens and become active only in the duodenum.
Recognize that any cause of acute pancreatitis, alcohol included, leads to activation of these enzymes inside the gland.
Identify trypsin as the key enzyme, because it activates the other zymogens.
questions.why: Acute pancreatitis begins when trypsinogen is activated to trypsin inside acinar cells or ducts. Trypsin then activates the other zymogens, such as phospholipase A2 and elastase, and these enzymes digest the gland, its fat, and its blood vessels. Alcohol promotes this by thickening pancreatic secretions so they plug small ducts, by directly injuring acinar cells, and by causing abnormal enzyme release. Gallstones and alcohol cause most cases, with hypertriglyceridemia, hypercalcemia, ERCP, mumps, trauma, and some drugs such as thiazides as less common causes.
whyNot: Correct.
Islet hormones do not digest tissue. Islet damage may follow severe necrosis, but it is a result of the injury, not its cause.
Bile reflux through a shared channel is one proposed way that a gallstone at the ampulla triggers pancreatitis. Even then, the injury runs through trypsin activation, and he has no gallstones.
IgG4-positive plasma cells mark autoimmune pancreatitis, which causes a painless, diffusely enlarged pancreas and responds to glucocorticoids.

questions.stem: The fluid collection seen 5 weeks later is drained, and part of its wall is examined microscopically. Which of the following findings is most likely?
options: Columnar mucinous epithelium over ovarian-type stroma
Glycogen-rich cuboidal epithelium lining many small cysts
Fibrous granulation tissue with no epithelial lining
Papillary mucinous epithelium lining dilated main ducts
approach: Recognize the complication: a well-defined fluid collection in the lesser sac several weeks after acute pancreatitis is a pseudocyst.
Recall why it is called a pseudocyst: the wall is reactive tissue, not epithelium.
Exclude the cystic neoplasms, which all have an epithelial lining.
questions.why: A pancreatic pseudocyst forms when enzyme-rich fluid and necrotic debris from pancreatitis are walled off, often in the lesser sac. Over about 4 weeks the body builds a wall of granulation tissue that matures into fibrous tissue. There is no epithelial lining, which is what makes it a pseudocyst. Large pseudocysts can press on the stomach and cause early satiety, and they can become infected, bleed, or rupture.
whyNot: Mucinous epithelium over ovarian-type stroma defines a mucinous cystic neoplasm, which occurs almost only in women, usually in the body or tail, and has malignant potential.
Glycogen-rich cuboidal cells lining many small cysts describe a serous cystadenoma, a benign tumor usually seen in older women.
Correct.
Papillary mucin-producing epithelium in dilated ducts describes an intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm, a precursor of pancreatic cancer.

questions.stem: His initial CT shows peripancreatic fluid confined behind the posterior parietal peritoneum. Which of the following structures is most likely to be surrounded by this fluid?
options: Proximal first part of the duodenum
Second part of the duodenum
Proximal jejunum
Lower pole of the spleen
approach: Recognize that fluid behind the posterior parietal peritoneum lies in the retroperitoneum, where most of the pancreas sits.
Sort the options into intraperitoneal and retroperitoneal structures.
Pick the only retroperitoneal one: the descending duodenum, which curves around the pancreatic head.
questions.why: The pancreas, except for its tail, is a secondarily retroperitoneal organ. The duodenum from its second to fourth parts, the ascending and descending colon, and part of the rectum share this location, along with the kidneys, ureters, adrenal glands, aorta, and inferior vena cava. Inflammatory fluid from pancreatitis spreads through these retroperitoneal spaces and can surround the duodenum and reach the flanks.
whyNot: The proximal first part of the duodenum (the bulb, about 2 cm) has a mesentery and is intraperitoneal. The rest of the duodenum is retroperitoneal.
Correct.
The jejunum hangs on the mesentery and is intraperitoneal. Fluid would reach it only by spreading into the peritoneal cavity.
The spleen is intraperitoneal, held by the gastrosplenic and splenorenal ligaments. The pancreatic tail reaches it within the splenorenal ligament.

questions.stem: When he resumes eating, a meal delivers fatty acids and amino acids to his duodenum. Which of the following hormones, with its source cell, most directly increases pancreatic enzyme secretion in response?
options: Secretin from S cells
Gastrin from G cells
Glucose-dependent insulinotropic peptide from K cells
Cholecystokinin from I cells
approach: Identify the stimulus: fat and protein products in the duodenum.
Recall which duodenal hormone responds to fat and amino acids and which responds to acid.
Match enzyme secretion from acinar cells to cholecystokinin, made by I cells.
questions.why: Fatty acids, monoglycerides, and amino acids in the duodenum and jejunum stimulate I cells to release cholecystokinin. CCK acts on acinar cells, largely through vagal reflexes, to release digestive enzymes, and it contracts the gallbladder and relaxes the sphincter of Oddi. It also slows gastric emptying. Acid entering the duodenum instead triggers secretin from S cells, which drives bicarbonate secretion from duct cells. Patients with acute pancreatitis are often kept from eating at first so that this stimulation is avoided.
whyNot: Secretin from duodenal S cells responds mainly to acid and stimulates duct cells to secrete bicarbonate-rich fluid, not enzymes.
Gastrin from antral G cells responds to peptides and amino acids in the stomach and stimulates gastric acid secretion.
GIP from K cells responds to glucose and fat and increases insulin release. It does not drive enzyme secretion.
Correct.

topics: GI hormones and their source cells

dx: Hypertriglyceridemia-induced acute pancreatitis with steatotic liver disease
case: A 38-year-old woman with obesity and type 2 diabetes mellitus is brought to the emergency department because of an 8-hour history of severe epigastric pain radiating to the back and repeated vomiting. She rarely drinks alcohol. Her BMI is 36 kg/m2. Temperature is 37.9 °C (100.2 °F), pulse is 108/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 112/70 mm Hg. Physical examination shows epigastric tenderness. Her plasma is visibly milky. Laboratory studies show serum lipase 2400 U/L (normal 10 to 140), triglycerides 2150 mg/dL (normal below 150), glucose 248 mg/dL (normal fasting 70 to 99), ALT 68 U/L (normal 10 to 40), and AST 49 U/L (normal 10 to 40). Ultrasonography shows no gallstones and a diffusely echogenic liver. Diagnosis: hypertriglyceridemia-induced acute pancreatitis with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease.

questions.stem: On hospital day 2, she has perioral tingling, and her serum calcium concentration is 7.4 mg/dL (normal 8.5 to 10.5). Which of the following best explains this finding?
options: Reduced intestinal calcium absorption from vitamin D deficiency
Increased urinary calcium loss from renal tubular injury
Calcium uptake into bone driven by excess calcitonin
Calcium binding to fatty acids released in peripancreatic fat
approach: Recall that pancreatic lipase leaks into the fat around the pancreas during acute pancreatitis.
Follow the chemistry: lipase splits triglyceride into free fatty acids, which bind calcium.
Link calcium soap formation to a falling serum calcium.
questions.why: In acute pancreatitis, activated lipase escapes into peripancreatic and omental fat and splits triglycerides into free fatty acids. The fatty acids combine with calcium to form insoluble calcium soaps, seen as chalky white spots of fat necrosis. This takes calcium out of the blood, and a low calcium is a sign of more severe disease. Other classic findings are epigastric pain radiating to the back, lipase above 3 times normal, and in hemorrhagic disease, periumbilical (Cullen) or flank (Grey Turner) bruising.
whyNot: Vitamin D deficiency lowers calcium over weeks to months. It does not explain a fall within 2 days of acute pancreatitis.
Tubular injury is not a usual cause of hypocalcemia here. Calcium falls because it is deposited in necrotic fat.
Calcitonin has only a small effect on serum calcium in adults and is not raised in pancreatitis.
Correct.

questions.stem: Dietary triglyceride reaches her blood in chylomicrons that enterocytes assemble with apolipoprotein B-48. A child with a mutation that prevents enterocytes from loading lipid onto apolipoprotein B would most likely have which of the following?
options: Eruptive xanthomas, lipemia retinalis, and recurrent pancreatitis
Steatorrhea, acanthocytes, and ataxia from vitamin E deficiency
Tendon xanthomas and early coronary artery disease
Enlarged orange tonsils and very low HDL cholesterol
approach: Trace fat absorption: micelles deliver fatty acids and monoglycerides to enterocytes, which re-form triglyceride and package it with apoB-48 into chylomicrons that enter lacteals.
Recognize the defect: without microsomal triglyceride transfer protein, chylomicrons cannot form (abetalipoproteinemia).
Predict the result: fat stays in enterocytes and is lost in the stool, and fat-soluble vitamins, especially vitamin E, are not absorbed.
questions.why: After bile salt micelles deliver fatty acids and monoglycerides to the enterocyte, the cell re-forms triglyceride in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum. Microsomal triglyceride transfer protein loads this lipid onto apoB-48 to form chylomicrons, which leave through lacteals into the lymph. In abetalipoproteinemia, MTP is absent, so no chylomicrons or VLDL form. Fat builds up in enterocytes and is lost as steatorrhea, red cells develop spiky membranes (acanthocytes), and vitamin E deficiency damages the spinal cord and retina.
whyNot: This triad comes from lipoprotein lipase or apoC-II deficiency. Chylomicrons form normally but are not cleared from the blood, much like her own hypertriglyceridemia. In the child described, chylomicrons cannot form at all.
Correct.
Tendon xanthomas and early coronary disease come from familial hypercholesterolemia, a defect in the LDL receptor or apoB-100 binding.
Orange tonsils with very low HDL describe Tangier disease, a defect in the ABCA1 cholesterol transporter.

questions.stem: Which of the following mechanisms most directly links her insulin resistance to the accumulation of triglyceride in her hepatocytes?
options: Increased export of hepatocyte triglyceride as VLDL
Decreased hepatic fatty acid synthesis from glucose
Increased fatty acid release from adipose tissue lipolysis
Increased hepatic beta-oxidation of fatty acids in mitochondria
approach: Recall that insulin normally suppresses lipolysis in adipose tissue.
Predict what happens when adipose tissue resists insulin: more free fatty acids flow to the liver.
Recognize that the liver re-forms these fatty acids into triglyceride faster than it can burn or export them.
questions.why: In obesity with insulin resistance, insulin fails to restrain hormone-sensitive lipase in adipose tissue, so fat cells release large amounts of free fatty acids. The liver takes them up and re-forms them into triglyceride, and high insulin levels also drive new fatty acid synthesis in hepatocytes. When intake exceeds what the liver can oxidize or export as VLDL, triglyceride collects as steatosis. Simple steatosis is fat alone. Steatohepatitis (MASH) adds hepatocyte ballooning and inflammation and can progress to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma.
whyNot: VLDL export removes triglyceride from the liver. More export would reduce fat, not cause it.
Hepatic fatty acid synthesis from glucose rises, not falls, in insulin-resistant states with high insulin levels.
Correct.
Beta-oxidation burns fatty acids. More of it would lower liver fat, so it cannot explain the accumulation.

questions.stem: In a healthy person, the pancreas secretes trypsinogen, chymotrypsinogen, and procarboxypeptidase as inactive precursors. Which of the following explains how all three become active in the duodenal lumen?
options: Enteropeptidase activates trypsin, which activates the rest
Gastric acid entering the duodenum cleaves each zymogen
Bile salts unfold each zymogen to expose its active site
Brush-border aminopeptidases remove the inhibitory peptide from each
approach: Recall the brush-border enzyme of the duodenum that starts protein digestion: enteropeptidase (enterokinase).
Recognize that it acts on trypsinogen only.
Follow the cascade: trypsin then activates the other zymogens and more trypsinogen.
questions.why: Enteropeptidase on the duodenal brush border cleaves trypsinogen to trypsin. Trypsin then activates chymotrypsinogen, procarboxypeptidase, proelastase, and more trypsinogen, so one brush-border enzyme switches on the whole cascade. Keeping these enzymes inactive until they reach the duodenum protects the pancreas, and a trypsin inhibitor made by acinar cells adds a second safeguard. Pancreatitis, as in this patient, starts when this protection fails and trypsin is activated inside the gland.
whyNot: Correct.
Pepsinogen in the stomach is activated by acid. Pancreatic zymogens are not, and duodenal acid is neutralized by bicarbonate.
Bile salts emulsify fat and help pancreatic lipase work, with colipase. They do not activate protease zymogens.
Aminopeptidases on the brush border finish digesting small peptides into amino acids. They do not activate the pancreatic zymogens.

dx: Chronic pancreatitis with exocrine insufficiency in cystic fibrosis
case: A 26-year-old woman with cystic fibrosis comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of bulky, greasy, foul-smelling stools and a 6-kg (13-lb) weight loss. She has had three episodes of acute pancreatitis since adolescence and has had intermittent epigastric pain since then. She does not drink alcohol. Her BMI is 17.8 kg/m2. Temperature is 36.9 °C (98.4 °F), pulse is 84/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 108/68 mm Hg. Physical examination shows digital clubbing, scattered crackles, and mild epigastric tenderness. Fecal elastase concentration is 62 µg/g of stool (normal above 200), and fecal fat excretion is 21 g/day (normal below 7). Fasting plasma glucose concentration is 132 mg/dL (normal 70 to 99). CT shows an atrophic pancreas with multiple calcifications. Diagnosis: chronic pancreatitis with exocrine insufficiency caused by cystic fibrosis.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains her raised fasting plasma glucose concentration?
options: Autoimmune T-cell destruction of pancreatic beta cells
Peripheral insulin resistance caused by obesity
Loss of islets as fibrosis replaces the pancreatic tissue
Excess glucagon secretion from an alpha-cell tumor of the pancreas
approach: Recognize chronic pancreatitis from repeated attacks, steatorrhea, and an atrophic, calcified pancreas.
Recall that ongoing inflammation replaces acini and later islets with fibrous tissue.
Link islet loss to diabetes, which appears after exocrine failure.
questions.why: Chronic pancreatitis is ongoing inflammation that replaces the pancreas with fibrous tissue, with duct strictures and calcifications. Causes include alcohol, cystic fibrosis, duct obstruction, and hereditary mutations in PRSS1 and SPINK1. Acini are lost first, causing steatorrhea and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency. As fibrosis advances, islets are also destroyed, so insulin and glucagon both fall, and diabetes develops. In cystic fibrosis this is called cystic fibrosis-related diabetes.
whyNot: Autoimmune beta-cell destruction is type 1 diabetes. It spares the exocrine pancreas and does not explain her calcified, fibrotic gland.
Insulin resistance from obesity drives type 2 diabetes. She is underweight, with a BMI of 17.8.
Correct.
A glucagonoma raises glucose and causes weight loss and a migratory necrolytic rash. It would not explain her calcified, atrophic pancreas.

questions.stem: Her CFTR defect has reduced the delivery of pancreatic enzymes to her duodenum. If her malabsorption goes untreated, which of the following is most likely to develop?
options: Prolonged prothrombin time from vitamin K deficiency
Megaloblastic anemia from folate deficiency
Microcytic anemia from failed duodenal iron absorption
Wernicke encephalopathy from thiamine deficiency
approach: Trace the defect: faulty CFTR reduces chloride and bicarbonate secretion by duct cells, so thick secretions plug the ducts and destroy acini.
Predict the result: too little lipase, so fat is not digested and is lost in the stool.
Recognize that vitamins A, D, E, and K travel with fat, so they are malabsorbed too.
questions.why: CFTR is a chloride channel in the apical membrane of pancreatic duct cells that also drives bicarbonate and water secretion. When it fails, pancreatic secretions are scant and thick, ducts plug, and acini are destroyed. Without lipase, dietary fat is not digested, so fat and the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K are lost in the stool. Vitamin K deficiency reduces carboxylation of factors II, VII, IX, and X, which prolongs the prothrombin time. CFTR defects in the gut and liver also cause meconium ileus in newborns and focal biliary cirrhosis.
whyNot: Correct.
Folate is water soluble and absorbed in the jejunum without pancreatic enzymes, so folate deficiency is not expected from pancreatic insufficiency.
Iron is absorbed in the duodenum without needing pancreatic enzymes. Iron deficiency suggests blood loss or duodenal mucosal disease such as celiac disease.
Thiamine is water soluble. Its deficiency is typical of alcohol use disorder or malnutrition, not pancreatic insufficiency.

questions.stem: Her chronic pancreatitis increases her lifetime risk of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma. In this cancer, the most frequently mutated oncogene encodes a protein whose mutation causes which of the following?
options: Loss of a CDK4/6 inhibitor that restrains the G1 to S transition
Constitutive tyrosine kinase activity from a gene fusion
Overexpression of an antiapoptotic mitochondrial membrane protein
Impaired GTP hydrolysis that keeps it in the active state
approach: Name the oncogene mutated in about 90% of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinomas: KRAS.
Recall that KRAS is a small G protein that is active when bound to GTP.
Predict the effect of the usual point mutation: GTP is not hydrolyzed, so growth signaling stays on.
questions.why: KRAS encodes a small GTPase that relays signals from growth factor receptors to the MAP kinase pathway. Normally it switches itself off by hydrolyzing GTP to GDP. Point mutations, often at codon 12, block this GTPase activity, so KRAS stays bound to GTP and keeps signaling. This is usually the earliest mutation in pancreatic precursor lesions. Pancreatic cancer is linked to smoking and chronic pancreatitis, and a tumor in the head of the pancreas typically causes painless jaundice with a palpable gallbladder (Courvoisier sign), weight loss, migratory thrombophlebitis, and a raised CA 19-9.
whyNot: This describes loss of CDKN2A (p16), which is also very common in pancreatic cancer. CDKN2A is a tumor suppressor gene, not an oncogene.
A fusion that creates a constantly active tyrosine kinase describes BCR-ABL in chronic myeloid leukemia.
Overexpression of the antiapoptotic protein BCL2 follows the t(14;18) translocation in follicular lymphoma.
Correct.

questions.stem: A biopsy specimen of her pancreas shows dense fibrosis with scattered remaining islets of Langerhans and a few residual acini. On hematoxylin and eosin staining, which of the following features identifies the enzyme-producing cells?
options: Pale cords of cells arranged around fenestrated capillaries
Basophilic basal cytoplasm and apical eosinophilic granules
Tall columnar cells with apical droplets of mucin
Cells with flattened basal nuclei and pale, foamy cytoplasm
approach: Recall that acinar cells make large amounts of secreted protein.
Link protein synthesis to abundant rough endoplasmic reticulum, which stains blue at the base of the cell.
Link stored enzyme to zymogen granules, which stain pink at the apex.
questions.why: Pancreatic acinar cells are pyramidal cells built for protein export. Their basal cytoplasm is packed with rough endoplasmic reticulum, whose ribosomal RNA stains strongly basophilic, and their apical cytoplasm holds eosinophilic zymogen granules full of digestive enzyme precursors. Islets of Langerhans are pale-staining clusters of endocrine cells arranged in cords around a dense network of fenestrated capillaries. In chronic pancreatitis the islets tend to survive longer than the acini, which is why exocrine failure comes before diabetes.
whyNot: Pale cords of cells around fenestrated capillaries describe islets of Langerhans, which release insulin and glucagon into the blood rather than enzymes into ducts.
Correct.
Tall columnar cells with apical mucin describe goblet cells or mucous duct epithelium, not enzyme-secreting acini.
Flattened basal nuclei and pale, foamy cytoplasm describe mucous acini, such as those in the sublingual gland.

dx: Alcohol-related hepatitis with a Mallory-Weiss tear
case: A 51-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of repeated hematemesis after a night of heavy drinking and forceful retching. He has drunk about a pint of vodka daily for 20 years and has had 3 weeks of increasing jaundice, anorexia, and right upper quadrant pain. Temperature is 38.0 °C (100.4 °F), pulse is 104/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg. Physical examination shows scleral icterus and tender hepatomegaly. Laboratory studies show leukocyte count 14,800/mm3 (normal 4500 to 11,000), AST 186 U/L (normal 10 to 40), ALT 72 U/L (normal 10 to 40), total bilirubin 8.4 mg/dL (normal 0.1 to 1.2), and prothrombin time 17.5 seconds (normal 11 to 13.5). Endoscopy shows a 1.5-cm mucosal laceration at the gastroesophageal junction and no varices. Diagnosis: alcohol-related hepatitis with a Mallory-Weiss tear.

questions.stem: A liver biopsy specimen from this patient is most likely to show which of the following?
options: Ground-glass hepatocytes containing hepatitis B surface antigen
Ballooned hepatocytes with Mallory-Denk bodies and neutrophils
Portal lymphoid follicles with mild macrovesicular steatosis
Granulomatous destruction of small interlobular bile ducts
approach: Recognize alcohol-related hepatitis: heavy drinking, fever, tender hepatomegaly, jaundice, leukocytosis, and an AST more than twice the ALT.
Recall the three histologic features of alcoholic hepatitis.
Match ballooning, Mallory-Denk bodies, and neutrophils to the key.
questions.why: Alcohol-related liver disease moves from steatosis to alcoholic hepatitis to cirrhosis. In alcoholic hepatitis, injured hepatocytes swell (ballooning degeneration), damaged keratin filaments clump into eosinophilic Mallory-Denk bodies, and neutrophils gather around dying cells. An AST to ALT ratio above 2 is typical because alcohol injures mitochondria, which hold much of the AST, and because alcohol-related pyridoxal phosphate deficiency lowers ALT more than AST.
whyNot: Ground-glass hepatocytes packed with HBsAg in their endoplasmic reticulum mark chronic hepatitis B infection, not alcohol injury.
Correct.
Lymphoid follicles in portal tracts with mild steatosis are typical of chronic hepatitis C infection.
Granulomatous destruction of small bile ducts is the lesion of primary biliary cholangitis, which mainly affects middle-aged women and causes cholestasis with a high alkaline phosphatase.

questions.stem: On hospital day 2, he becomes confused and has horizontal nystagmus, bilateral lateral rectus palsies, and an unsteady, wide-based gait. A deficiency of the cofactor for which of the following enzymes is most likely responsible?
options: Aminolevulinate synthase in heme synthesis
Prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases in collagen synthesis
Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase in propionate metabolism
Pyruvate and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenases
approach: Recognize Wernicke encephalopathy: confusion, ophthalmoplegia, and ataxia in a person with heavy alcohol use.
Identify the missing vitamin: thiamine, whose active form is thiamine pyrophosphate.
Recall which enzymes need thiamine pyrophosphate: pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase, and transketolase.
questions.why: Heavy alcohol use reduces thiamine intake, absorption, and storage. Thiamine pyrophosphate is the cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, which feed and run the citric acid cycle, and for transketolase. Without it, neurons in high-demand areas such as the mammillary bodies and the region around the third ventricle cannot make enough ATP. Giving glucose without thiamine can make this worse, so thiamine is given first or with glucose.
whyNot: Aminolevulinate synthase needs pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6). B6 deficiency, also common with alcohol use, causes sideroblastic anemia and seizures.
Prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases need vitamin C. Scurvy causes bleeding gums, perifollicular hemorrhages, and poor wound healing.
Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase needs vitamin B12. B12 deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia and subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord, which develop slowly.
Correct.

questions.stem: His prothrombin time stays prolonged after he receives parenteral vitamin K. Which of the following best explains the prolonged prothrombin time?
options: Reduced hepatocyte synthesis of clotting factors
Platelet sequestration in an enlarged spleen
Decreased release of von Willebrand factor from endothelium
Interference with the clotting assay by antiphospholipid antibodies
approach: Recall that the prothrombin time measures the extrinsic and common pathways, factors VII, X, V, II, and fibrinogen, all made in the liver.
Use the failed vitamin K response: if vitamin K deficiency were the cause, the prothrombin time would correct.
Conclude that the injured hepatocytes cannot make enough clotting factor protein.
questions.why: Hepatocytes make most clotting factors, including fibrinogen and factors II, V, VII, IX, and X. When liver cell function fails, factor levels fall, and the prothrombin time rises early because factor VII has the shortest half-life, about 4 to 6 hours. A prolonged prothrombin time that does not correct with vitamin K shows that the liver cannot make the proteins, rather than lacking the vitamin to activate them. Low serum albumin reflects the same loss of synthetic function, and failure of the urea cycle can also raise blood ammonia.
whyNot: Correct.
Low platelets cause mucosal bleeding and a long bleeding time, but they do not prolong the prothrombin time, which is measured in plasma.
Von Willebrand factor helps platelets adhere and carries factor VIII. Its deficiency prolongs the bleeding time and sometimes the aPTT, not the prothrombin time.
Antiphospholipid antibodies mainly prolong the aPTT in the laboratory while causing clotting in the patient. They do not explain liver-related coagulopathy.

questions.stem: Six months later, after another episode of forceful vomiting, he has severe retrosternal chest pain, and crepitus is palpated in the soft tissues of the neck. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
options: Rupture of submucosal esophageal varices
Recurrent mucosal laceration at the gastroesophageal junction
Transmural rupture of the distal esophagus
Herniation of the gastric fundus through the hiatus
approach: Recognize crepitus in the neck as subcutaneous emphysema, which means air has escaped from a hollow organ.
Recall that a mucosal tear does not let air out, but a full-thickness tear does.
Identify Boerhaave syndrome: transmural rupture of the distal esophagus after forceful vomiting.
questions.why: Mallory-Weiss tears are lacerations of the mucosa and submucosa at the gastroesophageal junction caused by retching. They bleed but usually heal on their own. Boerhaave syndrome is a full-thickness rupture, usually of the left posterolateral wall of the distal esophagus. Air and gastric contents escape into the mediastinum, causing severe chest pain, pneumomediastinum, and subcutaneous emphysema that can be felt in the neck. It is an emergency with a high death rate from mediastinitis.
whyNot: Variceal rupture causes massive hematemesis in patients with portal hypertension. It does not let air into the tissues, and his endoscopy showed no varices.
Another Mallory-Weiss tear would cause hematemesis but no air leak, because the muscular wall stays intact.
Correct.
A hiatal hernia can cause reflux and chest discomfort but does not release air into the soft tissues of the neck.

case: A 58-year-old man comes to the physician because of 2 months of right upper quadrant discomfort and a 7-kg (15-lb) weight loss. He has had type 2 diabetes mellitus for 6 years and chronic hand pain. Temperature is 37.0 °C (98.6 °F), pulse is 80/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 128/80 mm Hg. Physical examination shows grayish-bronze skin, a firm, nodular liver edge 4 cm below the right costal margin, and enlarged second and third metacarpophalangeal joints. Serum ferritin is 2850 ng/mL (normal 24 to 336), transferrin saturation is 82% (normal 20 to 50), and alpha-fetoprotein is 960 ng/mL (normal below 10). Hepatitis B and C serologies are negative. CT shows a cirrhotic liver with a 6-cm arterially enhancing right lobe mass. He is homozygous for HFE C282Y. Diagnosis: hereditary hemochromatosis with cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the excess iron in his body?
options: Low hepcidin, allowing high ferroportin activity in enterocytes
High hepcidin, trapping iron in enterocytes and macrophages
Loss of transferrin, leaving iron unbound in the plasma
Increased iron delivery from repeated transfusions of red blood cells
approach: Recall that the body has no regulated way to excrete iron, so iron balance is set by absorption.
Recall that hepcidin from the liver controls absorption by degrading ferroportin, the iron exporter on enterocytes and macrophages.
Recognize that the HFE mutation lowers hepcidin, so ferroportin stays active and iron absorption stays high.
questions.why: Hereditary hemochromatosis is autosomal recessive, and most cases are homozygous for the HFE C282Y mutation. HFE normally helps hepatocytes sense iron and make hepcidin. With low hepcidin, ferroportin on duodenal enterocytes keeps exporting iron into the blood even when stores are full. Over decades, iron builds up in the liver, pancreas, heart, skin, and joints, causing cirrhosis, diabetes, bronze skin, cardiomyopathy, arthropathy, and a greatly raised risk of hepatocellular carcinoma.
whyNot: Correct.
High hepcidin blocks iron export and traps iron in cells. This is the pattern of anemia of chronic disease, with low serum iron and low transferrin saturation.
Transferrin is not lost in hemochromatosis. His transferrin saturation is high because there is too much iron for the transferrin present.
Transfusional iron overload causes secondary hemochromatosis, as in thalassemia major. He has had no transfusions, and his genotype explains his disease.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old farmer from a region where stored peanuts and maize are often contaminated with Aspergillus flavus also develops hepatocellular carcinoma. A characteristic mutation caused by the mold toxin is most likely found in which of the following genes?
options: APC, which targets beta-catenin for degradation
KRAS, which relays growth factor signals as a GTPase
TP53, which arrests the cell cycle after DNA damage
BRCA2, which repairs double-strand DNA breaks
approach: Identify the toxin: Aspergillus flavus makes aflatoxin B1.
Recall how it becomes a carcinogen: liver cytochrome P450 converts it to an epoxide that binds guanine in DNA.
Recall the signature result: a G to T change at codon 249 of TP53.
questions.why: Aflatoxin B1 is a mycotoxin in moldy grain and nuts. Liver enzymes activate it to a reactive epoxide that forms DNA adducts at guanine, producing a characteristic G to T transversion at codon 249 of the TP53 tumor suppressor gene. Loss of p53 removes the checkpoint that halts damaged cells. Other major risk factors for hepatocellular carcinoma are chronic hepatitis B, which can cause cancer even without cirrhosis, hepatitis C, alcohol, and hemochromatosis. Alpha-fetoprotein is often raised, and the tumor spreads mainly through the blood.
whyNot: APC loss starts most colorectal cancers. Beta-catenin pathway mutations occur in some liver tumors, but they are not the aflatoxin signature.
KRAS mutations drive pancreatic and many colorectal cancers. They are not the hallmark of aflatoxin exposure.
Correct.
BRCA2 mutations raise the risk of breast, ovarian, prostate, and pancreatic cancer. They are inherited, not caused by aflatoxin.

questions.stem: His 50-year-old brother is also homozygous for HFE C282Y but has normal iron studies. Ten years ago, the brother had a Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, in which food passes from a small gastric pouch directly into the jejunum. Which of the following best explains his normal iron stores?
options: Food no longer passes through the terminal ileum
Food no longer passes through the duodenum
Intrinsic factor from the gastric body is lost
Colonic transit of dietary iron is faster
approach: Recall the main site of iron absorption: the duodenum and upper jejunum.
Recognize that a Roux-en-Y bypass sends food past the duodenum.
Predict that less iron is absorbed, which offsets the effect of his mutation.
questions.why: Dietary iron is absorbed mainly in the duodenum. There, ferric iron is reduced to ferrous iron, taken up by DMT1, and exported to the blood by ferroportin. A Roux-en-Y bypass routes food from the gastric pouch to the jejunum, so it skips the duodenum, and the loss of gastric acid also reduces conversion of ferric to ferrous iron. Iron deficiency is a common late effect of this surgery, and here it offsets his genetic tendency to absorb too much iron. Folate is absorbed in the jejunum, and vitamin B12 and bile acids in the terminal ileum.
whyNot: The terminal ileum absorbs vitamin B12 and bile acids, not iron, and a Roux-en-Y bypass does not exclude it.
Correct.
Intrinsic factor is needed for vitamin B12 absorption, not iron absorption.
Very little iron is absorbed in the colon, so faster colonic transit would not change his iron balance.

questions.stem: Three years before this diagnosis, he had fever, diarrhea, and severe right lower quadrant pain 4 days after eating undercooked pork. At surgery, the appendix was normal, and the mesenteric lymph nodes near the terminal ileum were enlarged and inflamed. A gram-negative rod was isolated from stool cultured at 25 °C (77 °F). Which of the following organisms was most likely responsible?
options: Listeria monocytogenes
Escherichia coli O157:H7
Shigella dysenteriae
Yersinia enterocolitica
approach: Link the clues: undercooked pork, right lower quadrant pain mimicking appendicitis, mesenteric lymphadenitis, and growth at cold temperature.
Recognize Yersinia enterocolitica, a gram-negative rod that invades through Peyer patches of the terminal ileum.
Note that iron overload favors this iron-hungry organism.
questions.why: Yersinia enterocolitica is a gram-negative rod spread by undercooked pork, unpasteurized milk, and contaminated water. It invades through M cells over Peyer patches in the terminal ileum and spreads to nearby mesenteric lymph nodes, causing pain in the right lower quadrant that can mimic appendicitis. It grows at refrigerator temperatures, which is used for cold enrichment in the laboratory. It depends on outside sources of iron, so patients with iron overload, such as in hemochromatosis, are at higher risk of severe infection.
whyNot: Listeria is a gram-positive rod spread by deli meats and soft cheeses. It also grows in the cold, but it causes sepsis and meningitis in newborns, pregnant women, and older adults, not mesenteric adenitis.
E. coli O157:H7 spreads in undercooked beef and makes Shiga toxin, causing bloody diarrhea and hemolytic uremic syndrome.
Shigella causes bloody diarrhea with colitis spread person to person. It does not cause mesenteric adenitis mimicking appendicitis.
Correct.

dx: Wilson disease presenting as acute hepatitis with hemolysis
case: A 17-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department because of a 1-week history of jaundice and fatigue. Her school performance has declined, and a hand tremor began 6 months ago. She takes no medications. Temperature is 37.2 °C (99.0 °F), pulse is 106/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 110/68 mm Hg. Physical examination shows scleral icterus, hepatomegaly, and golden-brown corneal limbal rings on slit-lamp examination. Laboratory studies show hemoglobin 8.9 g/dL (normal 12.0 to 16.0), reticulocytes 9% (normal 0.5 to 2.5), a negative direct antiglobulin test, total bilirubin 11.6 mg/dL (normal 0.1 to 1.2), direct bilirubin 3.1 mg/dL (normal 0 to 0.3), AST 182 U/L and ALT 96 U/L (normal 10 to 40), ceruloplasmin 8 mg/dL (normal 20 to 40), and 24-hour urine copper 410 µg (normal below 40). Diagnosis: Wilson disease with hepatitis and hemolysis.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains her low serum ceruloplasmin concentration?
options: Defective intestinal copper export limits ceruloplasmin synthesis
Ceruloplasmin leaks into the urine through damaged glomeruli
Ceruloplasmin is consumed by binding free hemoglobin
Apoceruloplasmin lacks copper and is rapidly degraded
approach: Recall the gene: ATP7B, a copper-transporting ATPase in hepatocytes, mutated in Wilson disease (autosomal recessive).
Recall its two jobs: loading copper onto apoceruloplasmin and excreting excess copper into bile.
Predict that ceruloplasmin without copper is unstable and degraded, so serum ceruloplasmin falls while free copper rises.
questions.why: ATP7B moves copper into the Golgi of hepatocytes, where it is built into ceruloplasmin, and into bile for excretion. When ATP7B fails, ceruloplasmin is secreted without copper and is quickly broken down, so serum ceruloplasmin is low. Copper that cannot leave in bile builds up in the liver, causing hepatitis and later cirrhosis. It then spills into the blood as free copper, which deposits in the cornea (Kayser-Fleischer rings) and basal ganglia, is excreted in large amounts in urine, and damages red cell membranes to cause Coombs-negative hemolysis.
whyNot: Defective intestinal copper export is caused by ATP7A mutations in Menkes disease, which leads to copper deficiency, kinky hair, and low ceruloplasmin. She has copper overload, with high urine copper and corneal rings.
Urinary loss of ceruloplasmin is not the cause. Her high urine copper reflects free copper, not lost ceruloplasmin.
Free hemoglobin is bound by haptoglobin, which falls in hemolysis. Ceruloplasmin does not bind hemoglobin.
Correct.

questions.stem: Copper is normally removed from the body in bile. In a different patient, obstruction at which of the following sites would most likely block both biliary copper excretion and drainage of the main pancreatic duct?
options: Cystic duct
Ampulla of Vater
Common hepatic duct
Minor duodenal papilla
approach: Trace bile: canaliculi, bile ductules, right and left hepatic ducts, common hepatic duct, then the common bile duct after the cystic duct joins.
Recall where the common bile duct meets the main pancreatic duct: the hepatopancreatic ampulla (of Vater), surrounded by the sphincter of Oddi.
Choose the site shared by both ducts.
questions.why: Bile leaves the liver through the right and left hepatic ducts, which form the common hepatic duct at the porta hepatis. The cystic duct joins it to form the common bile duct, which runs behind the duodenum and through the head of the pancreas. The common bile duct joins the main pancreatic duct at the hepatopancreatic ampulla, which opens at the major duodenal papilla in the second part of the duodenum, controlled by the sphincter of Oddi. A gallstone or tumor at the ampulla therefore blocks both bile and pancreatic juice.
whyNot: A stone in the cystic duct blocks only the gallbladder, causing biliary colic or cholecystitis. Bile from the liver still reaches the duodenum.
Correct.
Blockage of the common hepatic duct stops bile flow but lies above the pancreas, so pancreatic drainage is unaffected.
The minor papilla drains the accessory pancreatic duct, a minor route in most people. Bile does not pass through it.

questions.stem: Before the copper studies returned, the differential diagnosis included autoimmune hepatitis. Which of the following findings would have most supported autoimmune hepatitis?
options: Centrilobular necrosis after a large acetaminophen ingestion
Hepatitis that began 2 months after starting isoniazid therapy
Hypergammaglobulinemia and interface hepatitis with plasma cells
Steatohepatitis in a patient with obesity and insulin resistance
approach: Recall the profile of autoimmune hepatitis: usually young women, with autoantibodies such as ANA and anti-smooth muscle antibody.
Recall its laboratory and biopsy hallmarks: raised IgG and interface hepatitis rich in plasma cells.
Separate it from drug and toxin injury, which follows an exposure.
questions.why: Autoimmune hepatitis is a T-cell mediated attack on hepatocytes, most common in young women. Serum IgG is high, and ANA or anti-smooth muscle antibodies are often present. Biopsy shows interface hepatitis, in which lymphocytes and many plasma cells spill from the portal tracts into the nearby hepatocytes. It responds to glucocorticoids. Drug and toxin hepatitis follows an exposure and has its own patterns, such as zone 3 necrosis from acetaminophen and hepatitis from isoniazid.
whyNot: Acetaminophen overdose causes centrilobular (zone 3) necrosis through its toxic metabolite NAPQI. It would point to drug injury, and she takes no medications.
Isoniazid can cause hepatitis weeks to months after it is started. This would point to a drug cause.
Correct.
Steatohepatitis with obesity and insulin resistance describes MASH, a metabolic liver disease, not an autoimmune one.

questions.stem: Most of her serum bilirubin is unconjugated. Which of the following best explains this pattern?
options: Heme breakdown outpaces hepatic glucuronidation capacity
Inherited reduction in UGT1A1 gene transcription
Defective canalicular export of bilirubin glucuronides by MRP2
Bacterial deconjugation of bilirubin in the colon with reabsorption
approach: Recognize hemolysis: anemia, high reticulocyte count, and a negative direct antiglobulin test with copper overload.
Trace bilirubin: heme oxygenase and biliverdin reductase make unconjugated bilirubin, which travels on albumin to the liver for conjugation by UGT1A1.
Conclude that heavy heme breakdown, with an injured liver, produces more bilirubin than the liver can conjugate.
questions.why: Red cell breakdown releases heme, which macrophages convert to biliverdin with heme oxygenase and then to unconjugated bilirubin with biliverdin reductase. Unconjugated bilirubin is insoluble in water and travels to the liver bound to albumin. Hepatocytes conjugate it with glucuronic acid using UGT1A1 and export it into bile through MRP2. In the gut, bacteria convert it to urobilinogen and stercobilin. Her copper-driven hemolysis makes bilirubin faster than her injured liver can conjugate it, so unconjugated bilirubin dominates.
whyNot: Correct.
Reduced UGT1A1 transcription is Gilbert syndrome, a harmless cause of mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia with stress or fasting. It does not cause anemia or a bilirubin this high.
Defective MRP2 is Dubin-Johnson syndrome, which raises conjugated bilirubin and gives the liver a black color.

Gut bacteria can deconjugate some bilirubin, and a little is reabsorbed, which matters mainly in newborns. In adults most is reduced to urobilinogen and stercobilin, so this cannot produce her high unconjugated bilirubin.

case: A 44-year-old man comes to the physician because of 3 months of increasing abdominal girth, ankle swelling, and exertional dyspnea. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 20 years and rarely drinks alcohol. Temperature is 36.7 °C (98.1 °F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 112/70 mm Hg. Physical examination shows scleral icterus, spider angiomas, palmar erythema, shifting dullness, and splenomegaly. Laboratory studies show albumin 2.9 g/dL (normal 3.5 to 5.0), total bilirubin 2.6 mg/dL (normal 0.1 to 1.2), prothrombin time 15.8 seconds (normal 11 to 13.5), platelet count 88,000/mm3 (normal 150,000 to 400,000), and alpha-1 antitrypsin 22 mg/dL (normal 100 to 200). Viral hepatitis serologies are negative. Chest CT shows panacinar emphysema, worst in the lower lobes. His genotype is PiZZ. Diagnosis: alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency with cirrhosis.

questions.stem: His liver biopsy specimen shows round, PAS-positive, diastase-resistant globules in periportal hepatocytes. Which of the following best explains the formation of these globules?
options: Glycogen stored because of a debranching enzyme defect
Hyaline aggregates of damaged keratin intermediate filaments
Misfolded protein retained in the endoplasmic reticulum
Lysosomes filled with oxidized lipid from membrane injury
approach: Recognize the PiZZ variant: a single amino acid change (Glu342Lys) that makes alpha-1 antitrypsin misfold.
Recall what happens to misfolded secretory proteins: they polymerize and stay in the endoplasmic reticulum.
Use the stain: PAS-positive and resistant to diastase means glycoprotein, not glycogen.
questions.why: Alpha-1 antitrypsin is a glycoprotein made in hepatocytes and secreted into the blood, where it inhibits neutrophil elastase. The Z variant misfolds and forms polymers that cannot leave the endoplasmic reticulum. These polymers collect as PAS-positive globules that diastase cannot digest, because they are glycoprotein rather than glycogen. The retained protein injures hepatocytes and can lead to cirrhosis, while the low serum level leaves the lung alveoli open to elastase, causing panacinar emphysema that smoking makes much worse.
whyNot: Glycogen in storage diseases such as Cori disease is PAS positive but is digested by diastase.
Hyaline clumps of damaged keratin filaments are Mallory-Denk bodies, typical of alcoholic hepatitis.
Correct.
Lysosomes filled with oxidized lipid are lipofuscin, a brown wear-and-tear pigment that builds up with age.

questions.stem: Which of the following cells is most directly responsible for the fibrous septa that have converted his liver to cirrhosis?
options: Kupffer cells within the sinusoidal lumen
Fenestrated sinusoidal endothelial cells
Periportal hepatocytes containing the abnormal protein
Hepatic stellate cells in the space of Disse
approach: Recall that cirrhosis is bridging fibrosis with regenerative nodules.
Identify the cell that stores vitamin A in the space of Disse and turns into a collagen-producing myofibroblast after injury.
Name the hepatic stellate (Ito) cell.
questions.why: Hepatic stellate cells sit in the space of Disse between hepatocytes and sinusoidal endothelium, where they normally store vitamin A. Chronic injury releases cytokines such as TGF-beta from Kupffer cells and damaged hepatocytes, which activate stellate cells into contractile myofibroblasts. These cells lay down type I and III collagen, forming septa that bridge portal tracts and central veins. Surviving hepatocytes regrow as nodules. The main causes of cirrhosis are alcohol, chronic hepatitis B and C, fatty liver disease, and metabolic diseases such as this one.
whyNot: Kupffer cells are resident macrophages. They release cytokines that activate stellate cells, but they do not make the collagen.
Sinusoidal endothelial cells lose their fenestrations in cirrhosis (capillarization), but they are not the main source of collagen.
Hepatocytes holding misfolded protein are injured and die, which drives the process, but hepatocytes do not deposit the fibrous septa.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings in this patient results mainly from portal hypertension rather than from loss of hepatocyte function?
options: Congestive splenomegaly
Spider angiomas on the chest
Prolonged prothrombin time
Scleral icterus
approach: Sort the findings of cirrhosis into two groups: those from failing hepatocytes and those from high portal pressure.
Hepatocyte failure: jaundice, low albumin, coagulopathy, hyperestrogenism, and encephalopathy.
Portal hypertension: splenomegaly, ascites, varices, and caput medusae.
questions.why: Cirrhosis causes two kinds of problems. Loss of hepatocyte function leads to jaundice, low albumin, a prolonged prothrombin time, and hepatic encephalopathy, and poor breakdown of estrogen causes spider angiomas, palmar erythema, gynecomastia, and testicular atrophy. Scarring also blocks blood flow through the liver and raises portal pressure. Blood backs up through the splenic vein, so the spleen enlarges and traps platelets, and collateral veins open in the esophagus, rectum, and abdominal wall.
whyNot: Correct.
Spider angiomas come from excess estrogen because the failing liver cannot break it down.
A prolonged prothrombin time reflects poor hepatocyte synthesis of clotting factors.
Jaundice reflects failing uptake, conjugation, and excretion of bilirubin by hepatocytes.

questions.stem: Blood from his enlarged spleen normally joins blood from the superior mesenteric vein behind the neck of the pancreas. Which of the following sequences describes the normal path of this blood after that point?
options: Portal vein, central veins, sinusoids, hepatic veins, inferior vena cava
Portal vein, sinusoids, central veins, hepatic veins, inferior vena cava
Portal vein, sinusoids, hepatic veins, central veins, inferior vena cava
Portal vein, sinusoids, central veins, portal triads, inferior vena cava
approach: Recall that the splenic and superior mesenteric veins join behind the pancreatic neck to form the portal vein.
Follow portal blood into the liver: branches in the portal triads open into sinusoids, which run toward the central vein of each lobule.
Central veins drain into hepatic veins, which empty into the inferior vena cava.
questions.why: The portal vein forms behind the neck of the pancreas from the splenic and superior mesenteric veins, with the inferior mesenteric vein usually draining into the splenic vein. It enters the liver at the porta hepatis and branches with the hepatic artery and bile ducts in the portal triads. Blood from both vessels mixes in the sinusoids, flows past hepatocytes toward the central vein, and leaves through the hepatic veins into the inferior vena cava. In cirrhosis, resistance in the sinusoids raises pressure all the way back to the spleen.
whyNot: Central veins lie downstream of the sinusoids. Blood reaches them only after passing hepatocytes.
Correct.
Central veins drain into the hepatic veins, not the other way around.
Portal triads are where blood enters the lobule. Blood does not return to them after the central veins.

dx: Carbon tetrachloride hepatotoxicity in an industrial worker
case: A 36-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of a 2-day history of nausea, vomiting, and right upper quadrant pain, followed by yellowing of the eyes. Three days ago, she spilled carbon tetrachloride while degreasing metal parts in a poorly ventilated workshop. She drinks heavily on weekends. Temperature is 37.4 °C (99.3 °F), pulse is 102/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 114/72 mm Hg. Physical examination shows scleral icterus and tender hepatomegaly. Laboratory studies show ALT 3850 U/L (normal 10 to 40), AST 4620 U/L (normal 10 to 40), total bilirubin 4.2 mg/dL (normal 0.1 to 1.2), prothrombin time 18.0 seconds (normal 11 to 13.5), and creatinine 1.9 mg/dL (normal 0.6 to 1.1). Serum acetaminophen is undetectable, and viral hepatitis serologies are negative. Liver biopsy shows centrilobular necrosis with fatty change. Diagnosis: carbon tetrachloride hepatotoxicity.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the initial step in this solvent's injury to her hepatocytes?
options: Glucuronidation to a reactive acyl glucuronide metabolite
Cytochrome P450 conversion to a trichloromethyl free radical
Direct dissolution of hepatocyte membranes by unchanged solvent
Immune attack after the solvent binds hepatocyte proteins as a hapten
approach: Recall that carbon tetrachloride itself is fairly inert and must be activated by the liver.
Identify the activating enzyme: cytochrome P450, mainly CYP2E1, which forms the trichloromethyl radical.
Follow the damage: the radical starts lipid peroxidation of membranes.
questions.why: Carbon tetrachloride is the classic example of free radical liver injury. Cytochrome P450, mostly CYP2E1 in zone 3 hepatocytes, converts it to the trichloromethyl free radical. The radical reacts with fatty acids in membranes and starts a chain of lipid peroxidation that damages the endoplasmic reticulum, mitochondria, and plasma membrane. Damage to the endoplasmic reticulum halts apoprotein synthesis, so triglyceride cannot be exported as lipoprotein, and fat collects. Severe injury ends in centrilobular necrosis. Alcohol induces CYP2E1, so heavy drinkers are more vulnerable.
whyNot: Glucuronidation is a phase II reaction that usually detoxifies compounds. Acyl glucuronides form from carboxylic acid drugs, not from carbon tetrachloride.
Correct.
Carbon tetrachloride can depress the nervous system as a solvent, but liver injury needs metabolic activation. Damage centered in zone 3, where CYP2E1 is concentrated, shows this.
Hapten-driven immune injury causes some drug hepatitis that appears after a delay and often with rash or eosinophilia. Carbon tetrachloride injury is direct and dose-dependent.

topics: Carbon tetrachloride and free radical injury

questions.stem: Her physician notes that chronic heavy alcohol use also raises the risk of liver injury from acetaminophen. Which of the following best explains this added risk?
options: More NAPQI formed by CYP2E1 and less glutathione to conjugate it
Slower CYP2E1 activity that prolongs exposure to the parent drug
More glucuronide conjugates that precipitate within bile canaliculi
Higher glutathione levels that convert NAPQI into a toxic adduct
approach: Recall the usual fate of acetaminophen: most is safely conjugated with glucuronide or sulfate (phase II).
Recall that a small fraction is oxidized by CYP2E1 (phase I) to the toxic metabolite NAPQI, which glutathione conjugates and neutralizes.
Apply chronic alcohol: CYP2E1 is induced and glutathione stores are low, so more NAPQI is made and less is neutralized.
questions.why: Phase I reactions, mainly by cytochrome P450 enzymes, add or expose reactive groups. Phase II reactions join the drug to glucuronide, sulfate, or glutathione so it can be excreted. Acetaminophen is mostly handled by glucuronidation and sulfation, and a small amount is oxidized by CYP2E1 to NAPQI. Glutathione normally conjugates NAPQI. When glutathione runs out, NAPQI binds cell proteins and kills zone 3 hepatocytes. Chronic alcohol use induces CYP2E1 and lowers glutathione stores, so injury occurs at lower doses. N-acetylcysteine treats overdose by restoring glutathione.
whyNot: Correct.
Chronic alcohol induces CYP2E1 rather than slowing it. The parent drug itself is not the toxic agent.
Glucuronide conjugates are water soluble and excreted in urine and bile. They are the safe pathway, not the source of injury.
Glutathione neutralizes NAPQI. Higher glutathione would protect the liver, which is why N-acetylcysteine is the antidote.

topics: Phase I and phase II metabolism

questions.stem: She progresses to acute liver failure and receives a liver transplant. Two weeks later, Doppler ultrasonography shows thrombosis of the hepatic artery of the graft, with normal portal venous flow. Which of the following structures in the graft is at greatest risk of ischemic necrosis?
options: Periportal (zone 1) hepatocytes
Centrilobular (zone 3) hepatocytes
Sinusoidal Kupffer cells
Intrahepatic bile duct epithelium
approach: Recall the liver's dual supply: most blood flow comes from the portal vein, the rest from the hepatic artery, and both mix in the sinusoids.
Recognize that with portal flow intact, hepatocytes still receive blood through the sinusoids.
Identify the structure supplied only by the hepatic artery: the bile ducts, through the peribiliary plexus.
questions.why: The liver gets about 75% of its blood flow from the portal vein and about 25% from the hepatic artery, and the two sources each supply roughly half of its oxygen. Both empty into the sinusoids, so hepatocytes can survive on portal blood alone, which is why liver infarction is uncommon. The bile ducts are different. They are supplied only by arterial branches that form a plexus around them. After hepatic artery thrombosis, especially in a transplanted liver that has no collateral arteries, the bile ducts become ischemic and can necrose, leak, or narrow.
whyNot: Zone 1 hepatocytes sit nearest the portal triad and receive the most oxygenated sinusoidal blood. With portal flow intact they are well supplied.

Zone 3 hepatocytes are the most sensitive to a general drop in hepatic blood flow or oxygen, as in shock. Here portal blood still reaches the sinusoids, and the bile ducts depend entirely on the artery.
Kupffer cells line the sinusoids and are bathed in portal blood. They are not at special risk.
Correct.

topics: Dual blood supply of the liver
Arterial supply of the bile ducts

questions.stem: Her biopsy shows necrosis centered on the central veins, with surviving hepatocytes around the portal triads. Which of the following best explains why hepatocytes in the injured zone are most affected?
options: Highest oxygen tension and greatest glutathione content
Closest contact with portal blood carrying the absorbed toxin
Lowest oxygen tension and most cytochrome P450 activity
Most Kupffer cells, which release the toxic free radical
approach: Picture the hepatic acinus: zone 1 lies next to the portal triad, and zone 3 surrounds the central vein.
Recall that blood loses oxygen as it flows from zone 1 to zone 3.
Recall that zone 3 hepatocytes hold the most cytochrome P450, so toxins that need activation do their damage there.
questions.why: In the hepatic acinus, blood enters at the portal triad (zone 1) and flows through the sinusoids to the central vein (zone 3). Hepatocytes extract oxygen along the way, so zone 3 cells live at the lowest oxygen tension and are first to die in ischemia. Zone 3 cells also have the most cytochrome P450, including CYP2E1, so toxins that are activated by P450, such as carbon tetrachloride and acetaminophen, injure them most. Zone 1 cells, rich in oxygen, are the first hit by toxins that arrive directly in portal blood and need no activation.
whyNot: High oxygen and plenty of glutathione describe zone 1 hepatocytes, which survived here.
Zone 1 cells meet portal blood first. Toxins that need no activation injure zone 1 most.
Correct.
Kupffer cells are found throughout the sinusoids and do not activate carbon tetrachloride. The radical forms inside hepatocytes.
